chunks.content: 96 The Contract Clause That Could Outlive Your Deal Hi Sara, Let’s talk about a contract term that’s as exciting as it sounds- in fact, this is one of the only contract terms with a name that sounds more like it belongs in a dystopian thriller than a 40 page purchase agreement: Survival. Sounds intense, right? That’s because it kind of is. And let me tell you—if you’re negotiating a purchase agreement and glossing over the survival clause, you’re making a rookie mistake. What is “Survival”? No, it’s not a Hunger Games reference. In a contract, “survival” refers to how long your reps and warranties live on after closing. Here’s why it matters: If the agreement says nothing about survival? Those reps may hang around indefinitely (or until your local statute of limitations gives them the boot). That’s great for the buyer, not so great for the seller. The Seller’s Dilemma: If you're the seller, you don’t want to be on the hook forever. You want a survival period that caps your liability—12, 18, maybe 24 months. The Buyer’s Balancing Act: From the buyer’s perspective, you need some amount of time. You maybe won’t uncover shady vendor arrangements, ghost clients, or mysteriously disappearing revenue until you’ve gone through at least one full operating cycle. That’s why most buyers push for 18+ months—to uncover issues and have time to act on them. Pro Tip: If your contract says nothing about survival and you're the seller—fix that. Immediately. If it says nothing and you're the buyer—enjoy the gift that keeps on giving–at least through the applicable statute of limitations. Survival may sound like a footnote, but it’s actually a battleground in disguise. And if you want to fight smart, you better understand what you’re agreeing to.
